title: The Gentleman President Why George Washington Remains Our Timeless Example
author: Chris Martin
source: The Ways of a Gentleman (Martin Substack), February 16, 2026
summary: Martin holds George Washington as the quintessential modern gentleman, not for his military victories or political office but for his character—specifically his discipline, courtesy, courage, and restraint. At age sixteen, Washington hand-copied 110 rules of civility and lived by them throughout his life, treating all people with equal dignity regardless of station. Martin traces Washington's physical bravery (surviving fire at Monongahela with two horses shot beneath him) and moral courage (enduring Valley Forge with his men), but emphasizes his greatest act: voluntarily relinquishing power—refusing the crown offered after the Revolution and stepping down after two terms as president. In a world of self-promotion and division, Washington's example teaches that true strength lies in discipline, service, and knowing when to let go.
points: At sixteen, Washington hand-copied 110 rules of civility and actually lived by them—proving that deliberate self-education in courtesy and manners shapes a man's entire trajectory.

Washington showed both physical courage (withstanding intense fire) and moral courage (refusing a crown) because he understood that true leadership is quiet, steady duty fueled not by ego but by purpose.
His greatest act was stepping away: voluntarily relinquishing the presidency after two terms, establishing that power in a republic exists for service, not accumulation.
Washington maintained composure and respect even under intense provocation, demonstrating that a gentleman does not lose his temper, score points, or stoop to pettiness with rivals.

A gentleman pursues excellence in all areas—horseback riding, dancing, surveying, diplomacy—not as status symbols but as tools to move confidently through any setting and serve others more effectively.
quotes: I'm often asked who, among all the figures in history, I consider the ideal example of a gentleman. Given the vast expanse of time and the many great men who have graced the world stage, there are many options available. However, as an American citizen, I find it difficult to select anyone other than our nation's first President, George Washington.

Even as a young man, George Washington understood the importance of discipline, self-improvement, and manners. At the age of just 16, Washington hand-copied a set of 110 principles titled The Rules of Civility and Decent Behavior in Company and Conversation.

Throughout his life, Washington was known for his impeccable manners, calm demeanor, and courtesy toward others, regardless of their social standing. Whether dealing with foreign dignitaries, political rivals, or the everyday soldier in his camp, he treated everyone with dignity and respect.
At Valley Forge, where troops suffered from starvation, disease, and bitter cold, Washington's leadership was marked by compassion, resilience, and shared suffering with his men.

Perhaps no moment better captures his character than his response to calls for him to become king after the Revolution. In a world where victorious generals often crowned themselves rulers, Washington refused to take absolute power.” Archived from The Ways of a Gentleman (Martin Substack) on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
